children: By Mark R. Long

The maker of Lysol and Mucinex is doubling down on U.S. manufacturing and product development, the WSJ Logistics Report's Liz Young writes. Consumer-goods seller Reckitt Benckiser Group says it plans to invest about $400 million over the next four years in the U.S., building on a $200 million commitment made in 2024.

The additional investment is meant to speed up product innovation, help bolster its supply chain against disruptions and speed up its ability to meet spikes in consumer demand. The U.K.-based company bought a factory in Wilson, N.C., in 2024 to move some production of Mucinex cough and cold medicines from factories in Mexico and the U.K. to the U.S.

It now plans to double its investment in that plant to $400 million, including adding 234,000 square feet to the 310,000-square-foot building. Reckitt is also working to consolidate its commercial and research-and-development operations onto one campus in Nutley, N.J. And it plans to move its research-and-development teams focused on germ-killing products such as Lysol to that campus from nearby Montvale.
Quotable

"A year ago, our early demand driver was EV battery applications. Now, the focus is squarely on data-center and grid energy storage system battery applications."Eric McShane, co-founder and CEO of Electroflow Technologies, which is aiming to make it easier and cheaper to get lithium for batteries from salty water
Global Trade

The U.S. government is pressuring Mexican officials to accept new rules for exports of AI hardware to prevent Chinese companies and other foreign firms from circumventing tariffs, according to people familiar with the negotiations.

The Journal's Gavin Bade and Santiago Pérez write that the proposal would limit the amount of components that come from outside North America in the production of AI hardware. This set of products includes chips and servers and has quickly become Mexico's top export to the U.S., surpassing autos this year.

Mexico and the U.S. are discussing the so-called rules-of-origin proposal as part of negotiations around revising the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement, a trilateral free-trade deal that Trump has repeatedly threatened to abandon. While the U.S. has imposed tariffs on some Mexican goods, they largely remain much lower than levies on Chinese products.
The World Trade Organization said the splintering of the world trade system into geopolitical blocs or regional groups would curb economic activity. (WSJ)
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she would work to make Canada the bloc's first associate member. (WSJ)
Number of the Day

Average on-highway diesel price per gallon in the week ended Sept. 14, up nearly 32 cents from the week before and almost $2.55 from a year earlier, to a new record high, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration
Energy & Consumer Spending

American consumers have collectively spent about $107 billion more on gasoline and diesel during the Iran conflict and disruptions from the Russia-Ukraine war than they would have if there had been no war, the Journal's David Uberti writes.

That averages to more than $500 million a day since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, according to the Climate Solutions Lab at Brown University. A recent surge in crude indicates that the price tag will only grow in the weeks ahead. The Commerce Department, which forecasts more than $22 trillion in total personal-consumption expenditures this year, estimated that consumers spent more than $400 billion on fuel last year, not including businesses' diesel costs.

The Brown University model, which analyzes daily retail prices and historical demand patterns, estimates that cumulative gasoline spending this year has been $59 billion more than it would have been without the war. Additional diesel costs are roughly $48 billion.
Oil prices rose to four-month highs following the shutdown of Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline and Houthi threats to shipping in the Red Sea. (WSJ)
